passage:
Lena: I'm so full I can barely move. That last plate was a mistake.
Corbin: We paid $42 each for this buffet. Go get one more plate so we at least get our money's worth.
Lena: Making myself sick isn't going to get the $42 back, Corbin.
cue: We paid $42 each for this buffet. Go get one more plate
explanation: Corbin wants Lena to keep eating because of what they already paid. The $42 is spent whether she eats more or not, so the only real question is whether another plate helps her now.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Corbin isn't judging a claim by whether its outcome is pleasant; he's letting money already spent drive what Lena does next.

passage: Confession: I can't stand spin class. The music gives me a headache and my knees ache for days afterward. But I prepaid $900 for a full year of classes in January, so I'm dragging myself there four mornings a week until December. Not letting that money go to waste!
cue: I prepaid $900 for a full year of classes in January, so I'm dragging myself there
explanation: Jules keeps going to a class that hurts her knees because of money she can't get back. The $900 is gone either way; the real choice is about how she spends her mornings from now on.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Jules isn't continuing because it's how things have always been done; she's continuing because of what she already paid.

title: Re: Should we switch CRMs?
passage: Hi Noemi, thanks for the comparison sheet. You're right that the off-the-shelf option covers nearly everything we need for about $40k a year. Still, we've put eighteen months and $1.2 million into our in-house system. Walking away now would mean all of that was wasted, so I want to push on and finish it. Let's discuss Monday. Graham
cue: Walking away now would mean all of that was wasted, so I want to push on
explanation: Graham accepts that the cheaper tool does the job, then decides to continue because of the $1.2 million already spent. That money is gone either way; only the remaining costs should count.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Graham isn't defending the in-house system as the way things have always been done; his reason is past spending.

source: Mayor Delphine Achterberg · Port Ellery council session
passage: I've read the consultant's report, and I won't sugarcoat it: finishing the Riverside arena will cost another $30 million, and the operating forecast shows losses for at least a decade. But this town has already put $14 million into that site. We cannot let that investment go to waste. We finish what we started.
cue: But this town has already put $14 million into that site.
explanation: Delphine accepts the report's grim forecast, then argues to continue because of the $14 million already spent. That money is gone either way; the vote should weigh the $30 million still to come.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: Delphine doesn't dispute the report because she dislikes its conclusion; she argues for continuing because of money already spent.

source: Customer at the service counter · Pinchbeck Auto Repair
passage: I know, I know, the car's only worth about two grand and the transmission is another $2,500. But I put $3,000 into it this year already: new brakes, new tires, the alternator. If I scrap it now, all of that was for nothing. Go ahead and do the transmission.
cue: If I scrap it now, all of that was for nothing.
explanation: The recent repairs feel like a reason to keep going, but that $3,000 is spent either way. The real choice is $2,500 for a car worth about $2,000 versus the alternatives.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: The customer isn't rejecting a claim because its outcome feels bad; past repair bills are driving a decision about future spending.

title: Honest, patient, and knows the market
passage: Marisol was fantastic: honest pricing advice and gorgeous photos. She recommended listing at $435k based on recent sales nearby. But we paid $480k two years ago, and we're not taking a loss on our home, so we've decided to wait until the market gets us back to $480k, even if that means carrying two mortgages a while longer.
cue: we paid $480k two years ago, and we're not taking a loss on our home
explanation: Lucas and Mei anchor on what they paid, but buyers don't care about that number, and it can't be recovered by waiting. Their choice is today's price versus months of extra mortgage payments.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_consequences: They aren't rejecting the agent's advice as false because it's unpleasant; their reason to wait is the price they paid in the past.

title: Recommendation on the warehouse robot pilot
passage: Hi all, I know we've already spent $200,000 on the robot pilot, and that's painful. But that money is gone whichever way we decide. Finishing would cost another $500,000 for about $120,000 a year in savings, and the hardware lasts about three years. That doesn't pay back, so my recommendation is to stop here. Ingrid
cue: that money is gone whichever way we decide
explanation: Ingrid sets aside the $200,000 already spent and compares only what's ahead: $500,000 more for roughly $360,000 in savings over the hardware's life. Stopping follows from those numbers.

whyNot.fal_sunk_cost: Ingrid explicitly sets aside past spending and decides on future costs and benefits alone.

passage:
Carmen: Honestly, I'm sick of this renovation. Should we just stop and list the house as is?
Diego: Our agent says a kitchen without counters will scare buyers off, and finishing adds about $15,000 to the price. The counters cost $4,000.
Carmen: So forget the $40,000 we've already spent. That last $4,000 pays for itself. Okay, let's finish.
cue: finishing adds about $15,000 to the price. The counters cost $4,000
explanation: Carmen decides to keep going, but not because of past spending: she sets the $40,000 aside and finishes because the last $4,000 should add about $15,000 in value.

whyNot.fal_sunk_cost: The decision to continue rests on future costs and benefits, and Carmen explicitly sets aside what's already been spent.
